title: Round 5: Review a pull request and identify correctness, security and maintainability issues
description: Practice reviewing code the way a senior engineer does: spotting bugs, security risks, and maintainability problems in a realistic pull request.

data.text: The interviewer shares a short pull request and asks you to review it out loud. They want to see whether you can read code critically, explain issues clearly, and suggest fixes that respect the original intent. A good review is not a list of style preferences; it is a conversation about risk.

items.text: Does the code handle null, undefined, and empty inputs?
items.hint: Look for missing null checks or unsafe type assertions.
Unhandled promises and race conditions are common in API routes.
A PR that only covers the happy path is usually incomplete.

items.text: Does the change match the stated acceptance criteria?
items.hint: Mismatched scope is a frequent source of bugs.

items: User input is concatenated into SQL or log statements without parameterization
Authorization is checked after the sensitive operation instead of before
Secrets, API keys, or passwords are logged or committed to the repository
Dependencies are added without checking their license or maintenance status
Error messages leak stack traces or internal paths to the client
Passwords are stored or transmitted without hashing
CORS is configured to allow all origins in production
Rate limiting is missing on authentication endpoints

terms.definition: An attack where malicious SQL is inserted into input fields to manipulate or expose database data.
The process of verifying that an authenticated subject has permission to perform an action or access a resource.
A standard awareness document for the most critical web application security risks.
Every module and user should have only the permissions necessary to perform its function.

data.text: When you find an issue, describe the impact in plain language. Instead of saying 'this is vulnerable to SQL injection,' say 'an attacker could view any user's data by typing a crafted input here.' Interviewers notice when you connect the code to real-world risk.

data.title: Unsafe query example
data.content: A route that builds a query by concatenating user input is dangerous:

items: Are functions doing one thing, or are they long enough to hide multiple responsibilities?
Is the naming consistent with the rest of the codebase?
Are there duplicated logic blocks that should be extracted into a shared helper?
Does the PR include tests for new behavior and for edge cases?
Is the change documented in a way that future maintainers will understand?
Are there magic numbers or hardcoded values that should be constants?
Does the PR introduce new dependencies without discussion?

cards.title: Nitpicky style review
cards.description: Focuses on formatting, naming, and minor style inconsistencies.

cards.title: Risk-based review
cards.description: Prioritizes correctness, security, and data-loss scenarios.

cards.title: Pair review
cards.description: Two engineers review the PR together in real time.
cons: May miss issues due to groupthink

data.title: Assume the code will be attacked
data.text: Review every external input as hostile. If a PR ignores input validation or authorization, that is not a style nit; it is a security defect. Suggest a fix, but also ask whether the team uses a lint rule or automated scanner to catch similar issues in the future.

data.caption: Secure code review workflow from detection to prevention
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[New PR opened] --> B[Automated checks: lint, tests, SAST]
    B --> C{Human review starts}
    C --> D[Correctness scan]
    C --> E[Security scan]
    C --> F[Maintainability scan]
    D --> G[Comment: bug or edge case]
    E --> H[Comment: injection, auth, secrets]
    F --> I[Comment: naming, duplication, tests]
    G --> J[Author addresses comments]
    H --> J
    I --> J
    J --> K{All concerns resolved?}
    K -->|Yes| L[Approve and merge]
    K -->|No| M[Request changes]
    M --> J
    L --> N[Post-merge: deploy and monitor]

data.text: Modern code review combines human judgment with automated scanners. SonarQube, CodeQL, and Dependabot catch issues that humans miss—especially at scale. A senior engineer knows when to trust the tool and when to dig deeper.

data.title: Tools that augment human review
items: SonarQube: detects code smells, bugs, and security hotspots
CodeQL: semantic analysis for vulnerability patterns
Dependabot: alerts on vulnerable dependencies
ESLint/Prettier: enforce style and catch common errors
Secret scanners: GitGuardian, truffleHog for committed secrets

data.title: Review a real pull request
data.description: Find an open PR in a popular open source repository. Read the diff and write a review comment for each issue you find, categorized by correctness, security, or maintainability.
steps: Select a PR with at least one changed file and some existing discussion
Read the PR description and linked issue first
Inspect the diff for correctness issues
Inspect the diff for security issues
Write one comment per issue with a clear description and suggested fix
data.expectedOutcome: You should be able to write concise, actionable review comments that explain both the problem and the proposed solution.

data.title: Summary
points: Start with correctness: inputs, async flow, and acceptance criteria
Move to security: injection, authorization, and secret handling
Finish with maintainability: naming, testability, and documentation
Write comments that explain risk and propose a fix
Leverage automated tools but do not rely on them exclusively
data.takeaway: A senior review is a teaching moment. Explain why the issue matters, show a safer alternative, and keep the tone collaborative.
